Baby & Child

Atrioventricular septal defect: symptoms, repair and lifelong care

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Atrioventricular septal defect, or AVSD, is a heart difference present from birth that involves the central walls and valves. It is also called an atrioventricular canal or endocardial cushion defect. The exact anatomy determines how blood flows, when symptoms appear and what treatment is needed. A baby with breathing or feeding difficulties needs assessment, not a wait for a planned surgical birthday.

The heart’s chambers and valves

The heart has two upper chambers, the atria, and two lower chambers, the ventricles. The right side sends blood to the lungs to receive oxygen; the left side pumps it through the aorta to the body. Valves help keep blood moving forward. Normally, separate right and left atrioventricular valves connect the upper and lower chambers.

AVSD affects the central meeting point of the walls and these valves. Abnormal openings can send extra blood toward the lungs, and a valve may leak backward toward an atrium when a ventricle contracts. The heart must work harder; this is more than simply a small hole that can be assumed to close by itself.

Complete and partial forms

Complete AVSD usually includes an opening between the atria, an opening between the ventricles and one common atrioventricular valve. That valve may leak. The size and balance of the ventricles and other associated heart differences also affect the treatment plan.

In the usual partial form, an opening lies between the lower portions of the atria, while there are separate right and left valve openings. The left valve may have a cleft and leak backward into the left atrium. Transitional forms have additional features, such as a smaller ventricular opening; the echocardiogram defines the anatomy rather than the label alone.

Symptoms in babies and later life

Complete AVSD often causes symptoms in the first weeks or months: fast or difficult breathing, sweating during feeds, tiring easily, poor intake and slow weight gain. Wheeze, pallor, an abnormal heart rhythm or swelling may also occur. Blue or grey lips or skin can be serious; absence of blue colour does not rule out a heart problem.

Partial AVSD may cause fewer early symptoms and sometimes is found in later childhood or adulthood. Breathlessness, reduced exercise tolerance, tiredness, palpitations or leg swelling can reflect valve leakage, rhythm problems or increased lung-artery pressure. Symptoms alone cannot identify the defect, and new symptoms deserve clinical assessment.

When help is urgent

Get immediate emergency help for difficulty breathing, grunting or struggling for breath, sudden blue or grey lips, tongue, face or skin, chest pain, or a child who becomes limp, unresponsive or loses consciousness. A new fast or irregular heartbeat with illness, dizziness or fainting also needs emergency assessment. Follow the emergency service’s instructions; do not wait for the next cardiology visit.

If there are no emergency signs, contact the baby’s care team urgently the same day for declining feeding, increased sweating or tiredness, poor weight gain, new swelling or a concerning change from usual. Illness and respiratory infections can add strain, particularly with pulmonary hypertension. Use the individual cardiac plan, but seek urgent help if you cannot reach the team.

Causes, chromosomes and risk factors

AVSD develops while the heart is forming before birth. For many children, the precise cause is unknown. There is a strong association with Down syndrome, or trisomy 21, but AVSD can occur without it and a heart diagnosis does not by itself confirm a chromosome diagnosis. Genetic assessment and family-history discussion may be offered without blaming a parent.

Family history, pre-existing diabetes, some medicines, smoking and rubella are relevant to congenital heart-defect risk more broadly; they are not a checklist proving why an individual AVSD occurred. Medication and diabetes care should be reviewed before and during pregnancy, without stopping prescriptions independently. Avoiding alcohol supports pregnancy safety, but does not guarantee prevention of AVSD; no proven method prevents every case.

How diagnosis is made

A pregnancy ultrasound may raise suspicion, followed by a detailed fetal echocardiogram. A normal routine scan cannot exclude every heart defect. After birth, examination, a murmur or symptoms may lead to an echocardiogram, which shows the walls, valves and blood flow. A murmur may not be present at the first newborn examination.

An ECG evaluates electrical rhythm; oxygen measurements and chest imaging can provide other information. MRI or cardiac catheterization is selected when needed, including to clarify anatomy or pressures, rather than required for every child. Ask the cardiologist to explain the specific form, valve leakage, lung pressure and the next review or treatment step.

Repair and care before surgery

Most AVSDs require surgery. Complete defects are commonly repaired in the first months of life, sometimes earlier for symptoms; timing depends on anatomy, growth, valve function and lung pressure. A generic recommendation to operate sometime in the first year is not a reason to wait while an infant deteriorates. Partial defects also need an individualized repair plan, sometimes later.

Surgeons close the openings with patches or stitches and reconstruct the valves; in complete AVSD the common valve is usually divided into right and left valves. Complex anatomy may require a different or staged approach. Medicines and feeding support may manage symptoms before surgery, but do not close the defect. Discuss benefits, risks and recovery with the specialist team rather than assuming one operation guarantees a cure.

Complications and lifelong follow-up

Excess lung blood flow and valve leakage can enlarge the heart and cause heart failure or pulmonary hypertension. Untreated severe disease can permanently damage lung vessels. Treatment greatly improves outlook, but some people later develop leaky or narrowed valves, residual openings, abnormal rhythms or persistent pulmonary hypertension; additional treatment or surgery may be necessary.

Keep lifelong congenital-cardiology follow-up, including transition to adult care even when feeling well. Growth, feeding and developmental support may be needed. Activity advice is individual, not an automatic ban on play or sport. Good dental care matters; preventive antibiotics before certain dental procedures are needed only for selected circumstances, as the team advises. Keep a record of operations, medicines and the emergency plan.

Pregnancy with repaired or unrepaired AVSD

Many people with a successful repair and no important remaining problems can have a pregnancy, but a repair alone does not establish low risk. Before conception, an adult congenital cardiologist should assess valve function, heart pumping, rhythm and lung pressure and review medicines with the pregnancy team. If already pregnant, arrange that assessment promptly.

Significant valve leakage, heart failure, unrepaired disease or pulmonary hypertension can raise risk. Pulmonary arterial hypertension and some other severe forms of pulmonary hypertension carry high pregnancy risk and require specialist counselling. Discuss contraception, possible pregnancy risks and monitoring individually; avoid a blanket promise of a normal pregnancy or a decision based only on whether surgery occurred.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Current congenital-heart information distinguishes complete, partial and transitional anatomy and supports individualized early infant repair before permanent lung-vessel damage.

Repair is not the end of care: follow valve function, rhythm and lung pressure through childhood and adulthood.

Pregnancy planning needs an adult congenital-heart review; emergency symptoms must not wait for a clinic or app response.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize feeding or symptom notes, medicine lists and questions for the cardiac team. It cannot diagnose AVSD, interpret an echocardiogram, measure oxygen or lung pressure, or decide surgical or pregnancy safety. Seek urgent clinical care for warning signs even if an app record seems reassuring.

When to seek help

Call emergency services for breathing difficulty, sudden blue or grey colour, chest pain, loss of consciousness or a limp or unresponsive child. Seek same-day advice for concerning feeding, growth, sweating, swelling or other new changes without emergency signs. Do not alter cardiac medicines, feeding or fluid plans without the treating team.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • AVSD involves the heart’s central walls and valves; complete, partial and transitional anatomy differ.
  • Breathing difficulty, sudden blue or grey colour or loss of consciousness requires immediate emergency help.
  • Poor feeding, sweating, tiredness or poor growth in a baby needs prompt assessment; do not wait for a routine operation date.
  • Surgery improves circulation, but medicines do not close the defect and lifelong specialist follow-up remains important.
  • Down syndrome is associated with AVSD without determining every case; future pregnancy risks require an individual congenital-heart review.

Frequently asked questions

What are the symptoms of AVSD?

Babies may breathe rapidly, sweat or tire during feeds and gain weight poorly. Some partial defects cause later breathlessness, palpitations or tiredness. Breathing difficulty, sudden blue or grey colour or unresponsiveness needs immediate emergency help.

What causes it?

It develops before birth as the heart forms. The cause is often unknown; genetic and other factors may contribute. Down syndrome is associated, but AVSD does not by itself diagnose it or establish parental fault.

What increases the risk?

Chromosome conditions and family history may matter. Diabetes, certain medicines, smoking and rubella relate to congenital heart-defect risk generally, not a definitive cause of every AVSD. Seek individualized pregnancy and genetic advice; do not stop medicines yourself.

What complications can occur?

Extra lung blood flow and valve leakage can cause heart enlargement, heart failure and pulmonary hypertension. Even after repair, valve or rhythm problems may develop, so ongoing follow-up matters.

Will it close on its own?

Do not assume that. AVSD involves abnormal valves as well as septal openings and usually needs surgery. Medicines may ease symptoms but do not repair the structure.

When is surgery needed?

Complete defects are often repaired in the first months, with timing tailored to the child. Partial and complex forms have individual plans. New feeding or breathing problems require assessment rather than waiting for the planned date.

Is a child cured after repair?

Repair can greatly improve health and many children live active lives, but it does not remove every future risk. Keep congenital-cardiology reviews for life and discuss growth, development, activity and any new symptoms.

Can someone with AVSD become pregnant?

Often, but safety depends on remaining heart and lung problems, not simply having had surgery. Arrange pre-pregnancy adult congenital-cardiology assessment; pulmonary arterial hypertension and some severe pulmonary hypertension make pregnancy particularly high risk.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
